records.sourceFile: The Modified-Athletic Shoulder Test - Reliability and validity of a new on-field assessment tool.pdf

paper.citation: Tooth C, Forthomme B, Croisier JL, Gofflot A, Bornheim S, Schwartz C. The Modified-Athletic Shoulder Test: Reliability and validity of a new on-field assessment tool. Phys Ther Sport. 2022;58:8-15.
paper.abstract: Twenty healthy male athletes who played upper-limb sports performed the Athletic Shoulder Test on a force plate and a modified version using a handheld dynamometer, in two sessions seven days apart. Concordance and inter-session reliability were assessed in three arm positions, and scapular muscle EMG was recorded during the tests.
paper.tldr: The handheld-dynamometer version of the Athletic Shoulder Test agreed well with the force plate version in healthy upper-limb athletes, and the I position was the most reliable. Athletes should be familiarised with the test first, because strength was higher in the second session.
paper.methods: Test-retest and concordance study of 20 healthy male volunteers with a mean age of about 22 years who trained upper-limb sports about 8 hours per week. Isometric shoulder strength was measured in the I, Y and T positions with a force plate and a handheld dynamometer, in two sessions seven days apart. Upper trapezius, lower trapezius and serratus anterior EMG was recorded during the first session. Reliability was assessed with ICC, SEM, MDC95, paired t tests and Bland-Altman plots.
paper.findings: Concordance between the two tools was good to excellent (ICC 0.864 to 0.952) with no significant paired difference in any position. Inter-session reliability of the handheld version was moderate to good (ICC 0.643 to 0.923), with the I position most reliable (ICC 0.923); the MDC95 was about 39% of the mean in the Y position. Peak strength was 4 to 10% higher in the second session, significantly so for all positions with the force plate but only for the Y position with the handheld dynamometer.
paper.limitations: The sample was 20 men from mixed upper-limb sports, with no injured athletes, and EMG was measured only in the first session before familiarisation. The abstract gives a concordance ICC range of 0.86 to 0.97, whereas the results report 0.864 to 0.952, and some inter-session confidence intervals are wide (for example 0.233 to 0.849 for the handheld Y position).
paper.practicalImplications: A handheld dynamometer can be used on the field to repeat isometric shoulder strength measures, with the I position the most reliable if only one position can be tested. Familiarisation trials should be given before testing, and results from the Y position need caution because of high variability.
paper.athleteDev: Staff can use the handheld version to track isometric shoulder strength in overhead athletes, using the I position and a familiarisation session first. Interpret changes in the Y position cautiously, because day-to-day variability is large.
paper.rtp: The study tested healthy athletes only and did not compare the test with injury, surgery or return-to-play outcomes. It should not be used as a return-to-play decision tool on the basis of this study alone.

records.sourceFile: The Relationships Between Internal              and External Measures of Training Load and Intensity in Team      Sports-   A       Meta-Analysis.pdf

paper.citation: McLaren SJ, Macpherson TW, Coutts AJ, Hurst C, Spears IR, Weston M. The Relationships Between Internal and External Measures of Training Load and Intensity in Team Sports: A Meta-Analysis. Sports Med. 2017.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis estimated the correlations between internal load measures (sRPE, sRPE-TL and TRIMP) and external load measures (total distance, high-speed running distance, accelerometer load and sustained impacts) in team-sport athletes during training and match play. It also examined whether training mode moderates these relationships. Thirteen studies with 295 athletes and 10,418 session observations were included. Internal measures showed consistently positive associations with running and accelerometer-derived external loads, but their size and uncertainty depended on the measure and the training mode. The authors conclude that total running distance had the strongest association with internal load.
paper.tldr: Across 295 team-sport athletes, the pooled correlations between session RPE or heart-rate load and external load were all positive, but their strength depended on the measure and the training mode. Session RPE load (sRPE-TL) tracked external load more closely than heart-rate TRIMP, and total running distance was the external measure most strongly linked to internal load.
paper.methods: Systematic search of Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, MEDLINE, SPORTDiscus and CINAHL up to September 2017, following PRISMA, with two reviewers screening independently. Eligible studies reported a correlation between an internal and external load measure from team-sport athletes in unstructured training or match play. Studies with youth or injured athletes, experimental trials or non-category RPE scales were excluded. Random-effects meta-analyses (Knapp-Hartung 90% CIs, DerSimonian-Laird tau) were run for each dataset, and random-effects meta-regression examined training mode, with magnitude-based inferences.
paper.findings: Pooled correlations, all positive, were: sRPE-TL with total distance r = 0.79 (90% CI 0.74 to 0.83), with accelerometer load r = 0.63 (0.54 to 0.70), with impacts r = 0.57 (0.47 to 0.64), and with high-speed distance r = 0.47 (0.32 to 0.59). TRIMP with accelerometer load was r = 0.54 (0.40 to 0.66). sRPE with per-minute external measures ranged from r = 0.22 to 0.29, with unclear inferences. Training mode explained 24% of between-estimate variance for sRPE-TL with high-speed distance, and 100% for sRPE-TL with total distance and accelerometer load, and TRIMP with accelerometer load, in the models with enough estimates.
paper.limitations: Only data from healthy, non-injured adult team-sport athletes in normal training or match play were included, so the findings do not cover injured or youth athletes, and athlete sex is not reported. Heterogeneity was large for several relationships. Study designs were unstructured and observational, with varied GPS and accelerometer devices, sampling rates and correlation methods. Some studies pooled repeated sessions as one sample, which may inflate or distort correlations. Several datasets had few estimates, and some relationships could not be inferred. The authors also note possible mathematical coupling, since session duration is part of both internal and external load totals.
paper.practicalImplications: Monitor session RPE load (sRPE-TL) alongside total distance and accelerometer load rather than relying on one measure, since the authors say their data support using multiple measures. Avoid external-to-internal load ratios, which the authors say violate the assumptions of ratios because most of these relationships are disproportionate, and analyse continuous measures or changes over time instead. Compare sessions within the same training mode, because the links between load measures differ across modes, and consider collecting differential RPE to separate physiological from biomechanical load.
paper.athleteDev: Total distance and accelerometer load track session RPE load well in team-sport training, so the two can be read together to judge how hard a session was for players. Per-minute sRPE shows only weak links to per-minute external intensity, so it should not be used alone to judge session intensity.
paper.rtp: The review includes only healthy, non-injured athletes and excludes injured or returning players, so it cannot be used to set training loads during return to play.

records.sourceFile: The Reliability of Individualized Load–Velocity Profiles.pdf

paper.citation: Banyard HG, Nosaka K, Vernon AD, Haff GG. The Reliability of Individualized Load-Velocity Profiles. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2018;13(6):763-769.
paper.abstract: This study examined the reliability of peak velocity (PV), mean propulsive velocity (MPV) and mean velocity (MV) for building individual load-velocity profiles (LVPs) in the full-depth free-weight back squat. Eighteen resistance-trained men completed a baseline 1RM and three further 1RM trials 48 h apart, with loads from 20 to 100% 1RM. PV was reliable at all loads, MPV and MV were reliable up to 90% 1RM but not at 100%, and profiles from the reliable loads were highly correlated and did not differ between trials, velocities or fit types. The authors conclude that linear profiles from these reliable loads can be used to monitor velocity and adjust session loads according to daily readiness.
paper.tldr: In resistance-trained men, bar velocity measured at lighter and moderate loads was reliable enough to build individual load-velocity profiles for the back squat. Velocity at 100% 1RM was not reliable for MPV or MV and should be left out of those profiles.
paper.methods: Test-retest reliability study. Baseline 1RM back squat, then three 1RM trials 48 h apart, with repetitions at 20, 40, 60, 80, 90 and 100% 1RM. Velocity was measured with four linear position transducers sampled at 1000 Hz. Reliability used ICC, CV, Cohen's d and smallest detectable difference (SDD). Load-velocity profiles were fitted with linear regression and second-order polynomials, and correlations were compared with Fisher's r-to-z transformation.
paper.findings: PV was highly reliable at all six loads, including 100% 1RM. MPV and MV were highly reliable at 20 to 90% 1RM but not at 100% (MPV ICC = .66, CV = 18.0%, ES = 0.10; MV ICC = .55, CV = 19.4%, ES = 0.08). At 20% 1RM the SDD was 0.17 m/s for PV, 0.08 m/s for MPV and 0.06 m/s for MV. Individual profiles had correlations of r = .89 to .99 (PV), .90 to .99 (MPV) and .90 to .99 (MV). Linear and polynomial fits, the three velocities and the trials did not differ significantly. Group 1RM reliability was high (ICC = .99, CV = 2.0%).
paper.limitations: Only 18 resistance-trained men, all tested on one exercise, with three trials 48 h apart. Reliability is not tested over longer periods or during training. The stated reliability criteria differ slightly between the Methods (moderate CV of 10% or more) and the abstract (CV of 10% or less), and the abstract's group-level correlation ranges are not shown in the Results, which report individual profile correlations of .89 to .99. The findings apply to free-weight back squats with a set depth and maximal concentric effort. The authors note that results may not transfer to other exercises.
paper.practicalImplications: Before using load-velocity profiling for back squats, run a 1RM test, build each athlete's own profile from PV at 20 to 100% 1RM or MPV or MV at 20 to 90% 1RM, and fit a linear regression. Keep the velocity at 100% 1RM out of MPV and MV profiles. Change loads only when a velocity falls outside the smallest detectable difference for that measure, and only when bar displacement and maximal concentric effort are kept consistent.
paper.athleteDev: Individual back-squat profiles built from reliable bar velocities at lighter and moderate loads can help decide whether a velocity drop is real. For example, at 20% 1RM a change of less than 0.06 m/s in MV or less than 0.17 m/s in PV is within measurement error, so it should not drive a load change.
paper.rtp: The study tested healthy, resistance-trained men and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to play, so these profiles cannot be used to judge readiness after injury.

records.sourceFile: The Thiol Oxidation State of Albumin Is Associated With Training Load Across an Australian Football Pre-Season.pdf

paper.citation: James C, Weber J, Boyde C, Fournier PA, Arthur PG. The Thiol Oxidation State of Albumin Is Associated With Training Load Across an Australian Football Pre-Season. Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity. 2026;2026:5534194.
paper.abstract: A study of 45 professional AFL players from one team tracked a blood marker of oxidative stress (thiol-oxidised albumin) from daily fingertip samples across three pre-season periods. The marker was linked to GPS-measured running distance and change-of-direction running, and it was lowest during the COVID-reduced training block.
paper.tldr: A fingertip blood marker of oxidative stress (thiol-oxidised albumin) was higher in periods of higher running load in one AFL team. The link is modest, and the study did not test the marker against muscle damage or injury.
paper.methods: Observational study of 45 male professional AFL players from one team across three pre-season periods, one of them a COVID-affected block with training load reduced by about 40%. Players gave a morning fingertip dried blood spot before training at the three weekly sessions, and training load was measured with GPS units. Linear mixed-effects models tested links between the marker and GPS variables.
paper.findings: Thiol-oxidised albumin was higher in pre-season 1 than in pre-season 2 (p=0.012) and the COVID pre-season (p<0.0001), with no significant difference between the last two (p=0.25). It was associated with total distance (p<0.0001), distance at 10-20 km/h (p<0.0001), distance at 20-25 km/h (p=0.0082) and change-of-direction running (p=0.0025 in the total-distance model), with about 12% of variance explained (R2 = 0.12). Distance below 10 km/h and above 25 km/h were not associated with the marker.
paper.limitations: The single-team, observational design and small sample limit the associations, and the modest R2 leaves most variation unexplained. Muscle damage, injury and collisions were not measured, and training adherence during the COVID period was not verified. The Discussion gives p=0.0045 for distance at 20-25 km/h, but Table 2 and the abstract give p=0.0082; this summary uses the table value.
paper.practicalImplications: The paper suggests a fingertip blood test could give an indirect read on running load in a team. It is not ready for routine decisions, because samples were analysed in a university laboratory, the association was modest, and too few injuries occurred to test the marker against injury.
paper.athleteDev: Running distance at 10-20 and 20-25 km/h and change-of-direction running were the GPS measures linked to the marker, so these are the training-load components to watch if the marker is used. The marker followed training load across the pre-season, but it is not a tool for prescribing individual training yet.
paper.rtp: The study did not include injured players or return-to-play outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It cannot be used to judge whether an athlete has recovered from a muscle injury.

records.sourceFile: The Validity of Perceived Recovery Status as a Marker of Daily Recovery Following a High-Volume Back-Squat Protocol.pdf

paper.citation: Tolusso DV, Dobbs WC, MacDonald HV, Winchester LJ, Laurent CM, Fedewa MV, et al. The Validity of Perceived Recovery Status as a Marker of Daily Recovery Following a High-Volume Back-Squat Protocol. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2022. Ahead of print.
paper.abstract: Eleven resistance-trained men completed a baseline performance test and a high-volume back-squat protocol, then returned at 24, 48 and 72 hours to rate Perceived Recovery Status (PRS) and complete countermovement jump and mean bar velocity tests. Repeated-measures correlations showed strong within-person associations between PRS and both countermovement jump (r = .84) and mean bar velocity (r = .80), and the authors conclude that PRS can be used to assess daily recovery after a fatiguing resistance session.
paper.tldr: A single 0 to 10 PRS rating tracked jump and bar-speed recovery within individuals for 72 hours after a high-volume squat session. It may be a cheap daily check, but the same score meant different levels of performance recovery across people, so each athlete's own trend matters most.
paper.methods: Repeated-measures design in 11 resistance-trained men. Baseline countermovement jump (CMJ) height and back-squat mean bar velocity (MBV) were measured, then participants completed 8 sets of 10 back squats at 70% 1RM. PRS and the same performance tests were repeated at 24, 48 and 72 hours. Within-person repeated-measures correlations were used, with recovery expressed as a percentage of each person's baseline.
paper.findings: PRS fell from 8.3 at baseline to 4.6 at 24 hours and 4.8 at 48 hours, then rose to 6.2 at 72 hours. CMJ recovery was 84% of baseline at 24 hours and 85% at 72 hours; MBV recovery was 81% at 24 hours and 87% at 72 hours. Raw PRS was strongly correlated with CMJ height (r = .84) and MBV (r = .80), and with CMJ recovery (r = .84) and MBV recovery (r = .81), all P < .001. Individual responses varied widely, and PRS scores of 5 to 10 were recorded when objective recovery was 95 to 100%.
paper.limitations: Only 11 men were tested, with one exercise and one high-volume protocol, so generalizability to other training types, sexes, and athletes is limited, as the authors note. The correlations are within-person and do not show that a given PRS score predicts the same recovery across individuals. Baseline PRS ranged from 6 to 10, so baseline may not have been fully recovered.
paper.practicalImplications: Collect a PRS rating after the athlete has warmed up and track each athlete's own trend against what is expected for their training load, rather than applying one score cut-off to the group. A PRS trend lower than expected may prompt a review of load or recovery before overreaching develops. The same score corresponded to different objective recovery across people, so it should be read alongside other measures.
paper.athleteDev: PRS may serve as a daily, low-cost check on how an athlete is responding to resistance training load, with the athlete's own trend guiding whether to adjust volume or intensity. The study did not test whether PRS-guided changes improve performance or adaptation.
paper.rtp: This study tested recovery in resistance-trained men after one high-volume session, not injured or returning athletes. It cannot be used to judge return-to-sport readiness or to clear an athlete after injury.

records.sourceFile: The acute-chronic workload ratio and injury risk in semiprofessional football players.pdf

paper.citation: Seco-Serna R, Lago-Fuentes C, Barcala-Furelos M. The acute:chronic workload ratio and injury risk in semiprofessional football players. Int J Sports Med. 2024. Accepted manuscript.
paper.abstract: Prospective longitudinal study of 17 outfield players from a Spanish Third Division team over 24 weeks of the 2020/21 season, comparing session-RPE acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) with non-contact injuries. The authors found no meaningful association (rho = 0.069) and concluded that the ACWR alone is insufficient to predict non-contact injury in semiprofessional football.
paper.tldr: In one semiprofessional squad, a session-RPE acute:chronic workload ratio did not predict non-contact injuries, and it flagged only 5 of the 10 that occurred. The authors conclude the ratio should not be used as a stand-alone injury tool, while cheap session-RPE load tracking may still be useful.
paper.methods: Prospective observational study during the 2020/21 season in 17 outfield players, with data across 24 weeks (October to March). Session RPE (modified Borg scale) was recorded after every training session and match, and the EWMA ACWR was calculated with 7-day acute and 28-day chronic windows. Time-loss non-contact injuries were logged, and players were excluded from analysis while injured. Association was tested with Spearman correlation, and a 2x2 analysis classed an ACWR of 1.5 or above, or below 0.8, as a positive result.
paper.findings: Ten non-contact injuries occurred, 70% of them muscular, with an incidence of 5.91 per 1,000 hours and a mean of 11.9 days out. The Spearman correlation between ACWR and non-contact injury was 0.069 (N = 2,565), reported as very low. Five injuries occurred with an ACWR of 1.5 or above, or below 0.8, giving a sensitivity of 50%. The authors report specificity of 31.35%.
paper.limitations: Only 10 non-contact injuries (5 flagged by the ACWR) from one squad, so the estimates are imprecise. The abstract and discussion call the association non-significant, but Table 3 marks rho = 0.069 as p < 0.05, and Table 3 treats repeated player-day observations as independent. The 31.35% specificity equals the false-positive rate (801 of 2,555); the specificity from Table 4 is 68.7%, so that figure is misreported.
paper.practicalImplications: Session RPE is a low-cost load measure that clubs without GPS can collect, but this study found that the ACWR alone did not identify which players would suffer non-contact injuries. Treat the ACWR as one part of load monitoring, not a stand-alone injury alarm, and use other monitoring strategies as the authors recommend.
paper.athleteDev: Session-RPE load tracking is feasible in a semiprofessional squad without GPS. The study did not test whether ACWR-guided changes to training improve performance, so this use remains untested.
paper.rtp: The study did not evaluate the ACWR as a guide to return to play. Injured players were removed from analysis until they returned to full training, so the findings cannot be used to judge readiness after injury.

records.sourceFile: The association between alterations in redox homeostasis, cortisol, and commonly used objective and subjective markers of fatigue in American collegiate football.pdf

paper.citation: McKay BA, Delaney JA, Simpkin A, Larkin T, Murray A, Pedlar C, et al. The Association Between Alterations in Redox Homeostasis, Cortisol, and Commonly Used Objective and Subjective Markers of Fatigue in American Collegiate Football. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2021. Ahead of print.
paper.abstract: Observational study of 23 male student-athlete American college football players assessed over 10 weeks spanning off-season, preseason and in-season phases, examining associations between a point-of-care free oxygen radical test and defense test (FORT/FORD), urinary cortisol, countermovement jump (CMJ) variables and subjective wellness. Small associations were found between FORT/FORD and CMJ variables, sleep and soreness, and moderate associations were found between cortisol and CMJ concentric impulse and sleep. The authors suggest that routine subjective soreness assessment may be a time-efficient, noninvasive response measure.
paper.tldr: In one collegiate football squad over a season, a point-of-care redox test and soreness scores showed small links to jump performance and wellness. The authors suggest soreness questionnaires may be a cheap routine check, but the associations are small and the test's validity was not examined.
paper.methods: Repeated-measures observational study of 23 male NCAA Division I football players, with one assessment per week on a randomly allocated weekday over 10 weeks. Each weekly assessment included a fasted fingertip blood sample for FORT and FORD (used to compute the oxidative stress index), an overnight urine sample for cortisol and three CMJs on force platforms (flight time, RSImod and concentric impulse), and players also completed a daily morning wellness questionnaire for sleep, soreness and fatigue. Linear mixed models with random player intercepts were run, with effects standardized to a 2 within-subject SD change and interpreted with magnitude-based inference.
paper.findings: Small negative associations were found between FORT and CMJ flight time, fatigue and soreness (effect sizes -0.30 to -0.48). Small positive associations were found between FORD and CMJ flight time and RSImod, and between FORD and soreness. Cortisol had moderate positive associations with CMJ concentric impulse and with sleep (0.57 to 0.60). Greater soreness was associated with lower CMJ performance and with the redox markers, but not with cortisol.
paper.limitations: One team of 23 players in one season, with 39 models run and no correction for multiple testing. The abstract's effect-size signs conflict with the text (FORD-sleep is reported as +0.42 but described as a negative association), its conclusion that soreness is linked with increased cortisol is not supported by the Discussion, and the Discussion says cortisol was associated only with FORT even though the Results report moderate cortisol associations with concentric impulse and sleep. Samples were randomized across training days, so acute daily load effects were not controlled, and two authors consult for the company that supplied the FORT/FORD tests.
paper.practicalImplications: Routine subjective soreness scores can be collected cheaply and were associated with CMJ performance in this squad, so they may be worth including in monitoring. The FORT/FORD test is costly and its associations were small, so it should be used to support other measures rather than alone.
paper.athleteDev: Tracking soreness alongside CMJ may help staff notice when collegiate players are less ready to train. The study did not test whether adjusting load based on these measures improves performance or adaptation.
paper.rtp: Players were assessed during routine training and competition, and the study did not evaluate injured players or return-to-play decisions, so it cannot be used to judge readiness after injury.

records.sourceFile: The ballistic hip thrust test - A potential tool to monitor neuromuscular performance.pdf

paper.citation: Brown MA, Hader K, Guilhem G, Simpson BM, Buchheit M, Lacome M. The ballistic hip thrust test: a potential tool to monitor neuromuscular performance. Biology of Sport. 2022;39(1):73-77.
paper.abstract: This study examined the reliability of the ballistic hip thrust (BHT) test on force plates as a way to monitor posterior chain neuromuscular status, and compared its usefulness with the countermovement jump (CMJ). Twenty-two elite under-19 male football players completed two testing sessions one week apart, followed by a pre- and post-training comparison of the BHT and CMJ. Concentric mean force and takeoff peak force showed small-to-moderate typical errors, and the authors describe the BHT as having moderate reliability and usefulness, similar to the CMJ.
paper.tldr: A force-plate ballistic hip thrust gave moderately reliable force measures in 22 youth footballers, with usefulness similar to the countermovement jump. It may add posterior-chain information to a testing battery, but peak power was too variable (CV 40 to 58%) to rely on for monitoring.
paper.methods: Reliability and usefulness study on force plates. Assessment 1 used two sessions one week apart, each with three sets of four BHTs, and sets 2 and 3 were analysed for intra-day and inter-day reliability using typical error, coefficient of variation, ICC and smallest worthwhile change. Assessment 2 compared BHT and CMJ before and after a non-fatiguing training session, using signal-to-noise ratio (SWC/TE) as the usefulness measure.
paper.findings: Inter-day concentric mean force was 456 N and 477 N across days (CV 7.2%, ICC 0.88), and takeoff peak force had a CV of 12.7% (ICC 0.70). Intra-day CVs were 5.5% for concentric mean force and 4.2% for takeoff peak force (ICC 0.93 and 0.96). Peak power was unreliable (CV 39.8% intra-day and 57.8% inter-day; ICC 0.11 to 0.30). In the pre/post comparison, concentric mean force and takeoff peak force showed similar SWC/TE for the BHT and CMJ (for mean force, BHT 0.61 and CMJ 0.47), and the authors describe both as moderate.
paper.limitations: The sample was small and came from one club, and the authors note that a longer familiarisation period would likely have improved reliability. Fatigue sensitivity and injury-related use were not tested, and the BHT is hip dominant so it may not load the distal hamstring as Nordic exercises do. The abstract gives the intra-day CVs in the reverse order to Table 1 and the Discussion, and this review reports the table values.
paper.practicalImplications: Use BHT concentric mean force and takeoff peak force as an extra measure in a testing battery for posterior-chain monitoring, with a consistent warm-up and familiarisation. Peak power showed very high variability (CV 39.8 to 57.8%; ICC 0.11 to 0.30), so these data do not support using it for monitoring. Judge changes against the typical error and SWC, since most usefulness ratios were below 1.
paper.athleteDev: The BHT can complement a testing battery for weekly to biweekly monitoring of posterior-chain force (mean force and takeoff peak force) in running-based team sport athletes. Peak power's very high variability (CV 40 to 58%) means these data do not support it as a monitoring metric, and changes should be read against the typical error.
paper.rtp: This study tested healthy players and did not assess injured or rehabilitating athletes. It cannot be used to judge hamstring rehabilitation progress or return-to-play readiness, and the authors did not test fatigue or injury sensitivity.

records.sourceFile: The countermovement jump to monitor                                neuromuscular status- A meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Claudino JG, Cronin J, Mezencio B, McMaster DT, McGuigan M, Tricoli V, et al. The countermovement jump to monitor neuromuscular status: A meta-analysis. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2017;20:397-402.
paper.abstract: This systematic review with meta-analysis compared countermovement jump (CMJ) performance reported as the highest value with that reported as the average value for monitoring neuromuscular status, meaning fatigue and supercompensation. The authors included 151 articles and report that average CMJ height was more sensitive than highest CMJ height in detecting fatigue and supercompensation, with several other CMJ variables sensitive for supercompensation.
paper.tldr: Across 151 studies of CMJ monitoring, average jump height detected fatigue and supercompensation more clearly than the highest jump, while most other CMJ variables were rarely tested. Use it as a reason to average several trials, but the fatigue result rests on few studies.
paper.methods: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis following a search of PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science to 18 February 2015 for English-language studies that used CMJ to monitor fatigue or supercompensation after an intervention of at least three weeks in healthy participants. Effect sizes were calculated from pre- and post-intervention means and SDs, and coefficients of variation were calculated for each variable. Methodological quality was rated with a CONSORT-based checklist.
paper.findings: Of the 151 articles, 85.4% reported the highest CMJ value, 13.2% the average and 1.3% both. For fatigue, average CMJ height had an effect size of -0.56 (95% CI -0.89 to -0.24), while highest height was not sensitive (-0.04, -0.33 to 0.24). For supercompensation, height had an overall effect size of 0.37 (0.32 to 0.43), with 0.33 for the highest value and 0.74 (0.58 to 0.90) for the average. Peak power, mean power, peak velocity, peak force and mean impulse were sensitive to supercompensation, mostly in highest-value subgroups (mean impulse only just reached p = 0.05), and for power calculated from jump height only the average subgroup was sensitive.
paper.limitations: The fatigue analysis used five average-value and nine highest-value effect sizes, and 73% of CMJ variables were reported in only one or two studies. Acute studies (under three weeks) were excluded, and the authors say this may have influenced the results. Pooling across sports, ability and training status, and across force plates, position transducers and contact mats, may also have confounded the results. The authors could not determine whether the number of averaged trials changes sensitivity, and pooled participants were 80% male and 40% non-athletes. The highest and average comparison relies on separate pooled estimates, and the text reports no between-subgroup test statistic.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the average of CMJ trials performed without arm swing to track neuromuscular status, since average height was more sensitive than highest height in this review. Choose monitoring variables with a small-to-moderate CV and a moderate-to-large effect size, as the authors recommend, and treat fatigue signals with caution because the average-value fatigue evidence is limited.
paper.athleteDev: Use the average of several CMJ trials, without arm swing, to track fatigue and supercompensation, and prefer variables with a small-to-moderate CV and a moderate-to-large effect size. Jump height is simple to take from flight time, but the number of trials to average is not established and the average-value fatigue evidence is thin.
paper.rtp: Inclusion was limited to healthy participants, so the review does not show how CMJ responds after injury or illness. Its sensitivity results should not be used as return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: The current state of subjective training load monitoring - Follow-up and future directions.pdf

paper.citation: Coyne JOC, Coutts AJ, Newton RU, Haff GG. The Current State of Subjective Training Load Monitoring: Follow-Up and Future Directions. Sports Medicine - Open. 2022;8:53.
paper.abstract: Addresses how subjective training load is calculated (acute and chronic period lengths, smoothing methods and change measures), whether it can model sport performance, and where it fits in a practitioner decision framework. Examples use two datasets from elite athletes at the 2016 Olympic Games and linear mixed models, and the authors give practical recommendations such as validated scales and training athletes and coaches in their use.
paper.tldr: Subjective training load can be tuned for each sport and athlete by choosing period lengths and smoothing methods that fit performance data. Coaches should treat it as one input to decisions, not a rule that sets training.
paper.methods: A current-opinion article that builds on the authors' earlier practical perspective. Illustrative analyses use two previously published elite-athlete datasets (long jump and basketball), with Akaike Information Criterion variable selection across acute, chronic, change and taper measures, followed by linear mixed models with athlete as a random intercept. No systematic search is described.
paper.findings: In the long jump example, the best fit was a 9-day acute, 14-day chronic and 28-day taper window using SMA smoothing. In the basketball example, it was 9-day acute, 21-day chronic and 21-day taper using SMA. Training stress balance and its change before competition had the largest effect sizes in both mixed models (for example, change in TSB f2 = 0.313 for athletics and f2 = 0.192 for basketball). The authors report these as explanatory results from small datasets and not as validated models.
paper.limitations: The authors state that the two datasets are small, that the models were used for explanation only without training and test sets or cross-validation, and that they consider internal training load only. They also note that the type of taper and the location or severity of injury are not modelled, and no literature search method is described. The text gives p = 0.03 for the change in TSB in the athletics model, but Table 2 gives p = 0.01; this summary follows the table.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches should choose acute and chronic windows and smoothing methods by checking model fit against performance in their own sport or squad, rather than copying published windows. Subjective load should be used alongside readiness and external load measures, with validated scales such as CR-10 or CR-100 and athlete education on rating effort.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Staff can use session RPE and training stress balance to plan taper and week-to-week load, provided the windows are set from their own performance data and checked against model fit. The examples use elite athletes from two sports, so the specific windows should not be transferred to other teams without re-testing.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The paper does not address return to sport after injury. It discusses training load for healthy competing athletes and cannot be used to set load progression, clearance or return criteria after injury.

records.sourceFile: The effect of body mass on eccentric knee-flexor   strength assessed with an instrumented Nordic hamstring   device-Nordbord-in football players.pdf

paper.citation: Buchheit M, Cholley Y, Nagel M, Poulos N. The Effect of Body Mass on Eccentric Knee-Flexor Strength Assessed With an Instrumented Nordic Hamstring Device (Nordbord) in Football Players. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2016;11(6):721-726.
paper.abstract: Data from 81 soccer players (youth academy, 4th French division and professional) and 41 AFL players were used to examine how body mass affects eccentric knee-flexor strength measured with the Nordbord. Eccentric strength correlated largely with body mass, and the authors offer a regression equation to compare individual test results with body-mass-expected values.
paper.tldr: Nordbord eccentric hamstring strength rises with body mass, so a single absolute threshold may misclassify heavier and lighter players. Practitioners can compare an athlete's score with the body-mass-expected value from the reported equation.
paper.methods: Single-visit Nordbord testing (one set of three maximal Nordic hamstring repetitions, average of both legs) in 122 players from six groups, collected in season as routine monitoring. Body mass, skinfolds and percentage body fat were measured. Linear regression, log-transformed data, allometric scaling and magnitude-based inference were used. Players with an injury in the prior six months were excluded.
paper.findings: Across all players, eccentric knee-flexor strength correlated largely with body mass (r = 0.55, 90% CI 0.42 to 0.64); adjusting for body fat did not change the correlation. The regression equation is eccentric strength (N) = 4 x body mass (kg) + 26.1, with a typical error of about 22% (65 N). Absolute strength was highest in the professional soccer group (411 +/- 65 N), and only the professional soccer players were likely slightly (about 20%) stronger than their body-mass-expected values.
paper.limitations: This was a cross-sectional analysis of one test visit per player, so it cannot show test-retest change or injury prediction. Data came from six groups with different ages, standards and training histories, and the allometric exponent varied between them (0.57 to 1.51). Sex is not stated explicitly in the text. Individual differences smaller than about 40 N (12%) could not be reliably judged in a single test.
paper.practicalImplications: When comparing players of different body mass, or tracking one player whose body mass changes, staff can compare the Nordbord score with the body-mass-expected value from the reported equation. A single absolute strength threshold without body-mass adjustment may be misleading. The study gives no data on whether the adjusted values predict injury.
paper.athleteDev: Use the body-mass-expected Nordbord value to judge whether an individual's eccentric knee-flexor strength is below or above expectation. Differences under about 40 N (12%) in a single test should not be read as meaningful.
paper.rtp: This study cannot be used to judge return to sport or set clearance criteria. It contains no injured-player or post-injury data, and it excludes players with recent injury.

records.sourceFile: The fundamentals and applications of wearable sensor devices in sports medicine - A scoping review.pdf

paper.citation: Olsen RJ, Hasan SS, Woo JJ, Nawabi DH, Ramkumar PN. The Fundamentals and Applications of Wearable Sensor Devices in Sports Medicine: A Scoping Review. Arthroscopy. 2024:1-20.
paper.abstract: This scoping review of 43 studies from PubMed and EMBASE searches through 2023 characterizes wearable sensor devices used in sports medicine. The studies were grouped into athletic training, rehabilitation and research applications.
paper.tldr: Wearable sensors, mainly inertial measurement units, accelerometers and GPS, already measure workload, head impacts, biomechanics and recovery in athletes and patients. Their value for return-to-play decisions has not yet been shown longitudinally.
paper.methods: A scoping review following the Arksey and O'Malley framework and JBI guidance, searching PubMed and EMBASE through December 2023 with two independent screeners. Original peer-reviewed studies of wearable sensor use in sports medicine were included, and validation studies and reviews were excluded.
paper.findings: Of 43 included studies, 20 were in athletic training (mostly on-field IMU, head-impact and workload measures), 16 in rehabilitation (step count, gait, and return-to-throw monitoring) and 7 in research. Most studies used a single device, and sample sizes were typically small.
paper.limitations: No formal quality or risk-of-bias assessment was performed, and validation studies were excluded at the reviewer's discretion. Commercial head-impact sensors such as the X-patch and GForce Tracker can show measurement bias when a linear acceleration threshold is used, so video verification remains necessary.
paper.practicalImplications: Before relying on a wearable, confirm it has been validated for the specific metric, such as head-impact acceleration or step count, in a comparable population. Use video verification before acting on sensor head-impact counts for concussion screening.
paper.athleteDev: Use IMU or GPS data to track workload and movement mechanics within training, but check that the device is valid for the metric before using it to change training loads.
paper.rtp: Wearables can track return-to-throw progression, single-leg jump symmetry and gait during rehabilitation, but the review found no validated thresholds for when to return to play, so sensor data should inform clinical judgement rather than set the date.
